title: Places and directions
objectives: I can name common places in a Brazilian city.
I can ask where a place is and how to get there.
I can understand and give simple directions using vire, siga, atravesse and continue, and explain how those command forms are built.
I can say where things are using perto de, longe de, ao lado de, em frente a, atrás de and entre.
I can explain why the words of this lesson are spelled and accented as they are, including the accent on à.

vocabulary.note: Also means bench. The n only nasalizes the a: BAN-ku is [ˈbɐ̃ku], with no n sound (nasal vowels, first lesson).

example.pt: O banco abre às dez.
example.en: The bank opens at ten.
example.literal: The bank opens at-the ten.

vocabulary.note: Spelling: far-MÁ-ci-a is stressed on the third syllable from the end (counting the i of cia as its own syllable, as in história), and no ending predicts that, so the acute accent is required. It sits on an open a. The c before i is the s sound.

example.pt: A farmácia fica na esquina.
example.en: The pharmacy is on the corner.
example.literal: The pharmacy stays in-the corner.

vocabulary.note: Means market in general and, in everyday speech, the supermarket. An open-air street market is a feira. The c before a is the k sound, and the stress is on ca, the default for a word ending in o, so there is no accent.

example.pt: Eu vou ao mercado de manhã.
example.en: I go to the supermarket in the morning.
example.literal: I go to-the market of morning.

vocabulary.note: Spelling: the cedilla in ç is how Portuguese writes the s sound before a, o or u. PRA-sa, never PRA-ka.

example.pt: A praça é perto da igreja.
example.en: The square is near the church.
example.literal: The square is near of-the church.

vocabulary.note: The intercity bus terminal. Short for estação rodoviária, a station of the rodovia, the highway. Spelling: ro-do-vi-Á-ri-a is stressed on the third syllable from the end (the same pattern as farmácia), so the acute accent is required.

example.pt: Eu vou para a rodoviária de táxi.
example.en: I go to the bus station by taxi.
example.literal: I go to the bus-station of taxi.

vocabulary.note: Ponto means point or dot, and by extension a stop. The on in ponto is a nasal vowel. Ônibus is stressed on the third syllable from the end, so it always has an accent; the closed o takes the circumflex (accents lesson).

example.pt: O ponto de ônibus fica em frente ao banco.
example.en: The bus stop is across from the bank.
example.literal: The point of bus stays in front to-the bank.

vocabulary.note: Estação also means season of the year. The ç gives the s sound before a, and the ão ending is stressed by default, so the tilde needs no further accent. Metrô is me-TRÔ: it ends in o, which would default to stress on the second to last syllable, but the stress is on the last, so an accent is required, and the closed o takes the circumflex.

example.pt: A estação de metrô é longe daqui.
example.en: The subway station is far from here.
example.literal: The station of subway is far of-here.

vocabulary.note: The mail service, and by extension the building. Spelling: rr between vowels is the strong r, said like an English h. The ei is a diphthong, so cor-REI-o is stressed on rei and needs no accent.

example.pt: O correio fica perto do mercado.
example.en: The post office is near the supermarket.
example.literal: The mail stays near of-the market.

vocabulary.note: Spelling: h is always silent, and an l at the end of a syllable is said like w, so the word is oss-pi-TAW. A word ending in l is stressed on the last syllable by default, so there is no accent.

example.pt: O hospital é grande.
example.en: The hospital is big.

vocabulary.note: Spelling: g before r is the hard g, and j is always the zh sound, so i-GRE-zha. Stress falls on gre, the default for a word ending in a, so no accent is written.

example.pt: A igreja fica ao lado da praça.
example.en: The church is next to the square.
example.literal: The church stays at-the side of-the square.

vocabulary.note: Spelling: qu before e is the k sound and the u is silent. The final e is said i, so PAR-ki.

example.pt: Eu vou ao parque no domingo.
example.en: I go to the park on Sunday.
example.literal: I go to-the park on-the Sunday.

vocabulary.note: A loan word from English, kept in its English spelling, so it does not follow the ch rule: sh is the same sh sound as in English. The final ing is said as a nasal i, roughly SHOP-ee, and the g is usually not pronounced. Plural: shoppings.

example.pt: O shopping fica longe do centro.
example.en: The mall is far from downtown.
example.literal: The mall stays far of-the center.

vocabulary.note: A word-initial r is the strong r, said like an English h. The u and a are two separate syllables: RU-a.

example.pt: A minha rua é tranquila.
example.en: My street is quiet.
example.literal: The my street is quiet.

vocabulary.note: Stress is on ni, the second to last syllable, the default for a word ending in a, so there is no accent.

example.pt: Atravesse a avenida.
example.en: Cross the avenue.

vocabulary.note: Spelling: qu before i is the k sound and the u is silent: es-KI-na. This is the same rule that gives que and qui in the first lesson.

example.pt: Vire à direita na esquina.
example.en: Turn right at the corner.
example.literal: Turn to-the right in-the corner.

vocabulary.note: Distances are often given in quadras. Quarteirão is also heard. Spelling: qu before a is pronounced kw, so the u is not silent here: KWA-dra. Compare esquina, where the u is silent.

example.pt: A escola fica a duas quadras daqui.
example.en: The school is two blocks from here.
example.literal: The school stays at two blocks of-here.

vocabulary.note: In São Paulo people also say sinal. Spelling: se-MÁ-fo-ro is stressed on the third syllable from the end, so the accent is always required; the open a takes the acute.

example.pt: Vire à esquerda no semáforo.
example.en: Turn left at the traffic light.
example.literal: Turn to-the left in-the traffic-light.

vocabulary.note: The accent on à is the crase: the preposition a and the feminine article a have merged (see the contractions note). Direita is di-REI-ta: the d before i is said like the j of jeans, and ei is a diphthong.

example.pt: O banco fica à direita.
example.en: The bank is on the right.
example.literal: The bank stays at-the right.

vocabulary.note: Same crase as à direita. Spelling: qu before e is the k sound with a silent u: es-KER-da.

example.pt: A farmácia fica à esquerda.
example.en: The pharmacy is on the left.
example.literal: The pharmacy stays at-the left.

vocabulary.note: On its own it means ahead. With a and an object (em frente a) it means in front of or across from. Spelling: the n in frente only nasalizes the e, and te is said chi: FREN-chi.

example.pt: Siga em frente por duas quadras.
example.en: Go straight ahead for two blocks.
example.literal: Follow in front for two blocks.

vocabulary.note: Followed by de when it has an object: perto de. The r at the end of the first syllable varies by region.

example.pt: Meu trabalho é perto de casa.
example.en: My work is close to home.
example.literal: My work is near of house.

vocabulary.note: Followed by de when it has an object: longe de. Spelling: on is a nasal vowel, g before e is the zh sound, and the final e is said i: LÕ-zhi.

example.pt: A rodoviária é longe do centro.
example.en: The bus station is far from downtown.
example.literal: The bus-station is far of-the center.

vocabulary.note: Regular -ar verb. Its command form is vire (see the note on directions).

example.pt: Vire na segunda rua.
example.en: Turn onto the second street.
example.literal: Turn in-the second street.

vocabulary.note: Also means to go along or to continue on. Its eu form is irregular: eu sigo, você segue. The gu is written before e or i to keep the g hard; before o no u is needed. The command form is siga.

example.pt: Siga em frente até o semáforo.
example.en: Go straight ahead until the traffic light.
example.literal: Follow in front until the traffic-light.

vocabulary.note: Spelling: ss between vowels is the s sound; a single s there would be z. The command form is atravesse.

example.pt: Atravesse a praça e vire à esquerda.
example.en: Cross the square and turn left.
example.literal: Cross the square and turn to-the left.

vocabulary.note: Regular -ar verb: eu continuo, command continue. The ti is said chi.

example.pt: Continue até a esquina.
example.en: Continue to the corner.

vocabulary.note: An ordinal is a number that gives a position in a sequence. It is an adjective and agrees with the noun: a primeira rua, o primeiro semáforo. The ei is a diphthong: pri-MEI-ro.

example.pt: Vire na primeira rua à direita.
example.en: Turn onto the first street on the right.
example.literal: Turn in-the first street to-the right.

vocabulary.note: Feminine: segunda. Spelling: g before u is the hard g and the u is the vowel, so nothing is silent: se-GUN-do, with a nasal u.

example.pt: A farmácia fica na segunda quadra.
example.en: The pharmacy is on the second block.
example.literal: The pharmacy stays in-the second block.

vocabulary.note: Feminine: terceira. The c before e is the s sound.

example.pt: O banco é o terceiro prédio.
example.en: The bank is the third building.

vocabulary.note: Ficar literally means to stay or to remain, which is why it is the usual verb for the location of a fixed place. Fica is the você, ele and ela form of the regular -ar verb ficar; the c before a is the k sound.

example.pt: Onde fica o correio?
example.en: Where is the post office?
example.literal: Where stays the mail?

vocabulary.note: Chegar means to arrive, and the place follows em or a: chegar em, chegar na. Brazilians say chegar na praça. Spelling: ch is the sh sound, so CHE-go is SHE-goo.

example.pt: Como eu chego na estação de metrô?
example.en: How do I get to the subway station?
example.literal: How I arrive in-the station of subway?

vocabulary.note: Used to get the attention of a man you do not know, much as English says sir or excuse me. The feminine is moça. Spelling: the cedilla gives the s sound before o and a: MO-su, MO-sa.

example.pt: Moço, onde fica o banco?
example.en: Excuse me, where is the bank?
example.literal: Young-man, where stays the bank?

dialogues.context: Tiago is at the subway station and is going to Luiza's apartment for the first time. He calls her for directions.

dialogues.title: No ponto de ônibus
dialogues.context: Paula waits at a bus stop in the center of town and asks another passenger, Rui, for help.

lines.speaker: Paula
lines.pt: Moço, o ônibus vai para a rodoviária?
lines.en: Excuse me, does the bus go to the bus station?
lines.literal: Young-man, the bus goes to the bus-station?

lines.speaker: Rui
lines.pt: Vai, sim. Ele passa pela praça e pelo hospital.
lines.en: Yes, it does. It goes past the square and the hospital.
lines.literal: Goes, yes. It passes by-the square and by-the hospital.

lines.speaker: Paula
lines.pt: A rodoviária é longe do centro?
lines.en: Is the bus station far from the center?
lines.literal: The bus-station is far of-the center?

lines.speaker: Rui
lines.pt: Não, é perto. Fica atrás do shopping.
lines.en: No, it's close. It's behind the mall.
lines.literal: No, is near. Stays behind of-the mall.

lines.speaker: Paula
lines.pt: E onde fica o ponto para o metrô?
lines.en: And where is the stop for the subway?
lines.literal: And where stays the stop for the subway?

lines.speaker: Rui
lines.pt: Fica ali, ao lado da igreja.
lines.en: It's over there, next to the church.
lines.literal: Stays there, at-the side of-the church.

lines.literal: Obliged, young-man!

lines.speaker: Rui

lines.literal: Of nothing. The bus arrives soon.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: the words of this lesson
grammar.explanation:
Nothing in this lesson's spelling is an exception to the rules you already have. Every accent, cedilla and odd-looking letter pair follows from the reading procedure of the first lessons: divide the word into syllables, find the stressed syllable, compare it with the default for the word's ending, and, if they disagree, write an accent whose kind (acute or circumflex) is chosen by the vowel's quality, open or closed. The default is this: a word ending in a, e or o (with or without a final s), or in am, em or ens, is stressed on the second to last syllable; a word ending in anything else is stressed on the last syllable. A written accent says: this word is an exception to the default of its ending.

Accents on the stressed syllable. A stressed last syllable in a word ending in a, e or o (or as, es, os) breaks the default, so it is marked: lá, tá, pé, até and atrás carry an acute because their vowel is open, and metrô carries a circumflex because its o is closed. Words stressed on the third syllable from the end are called proparoxytones, and no ending predicts them, so they always have an accent: ônibus, semáforo, prédio, farmácia and rodoviária. In the last three, the ending is a glide plus a vowel (ia, io), and the i counts as its own syllable, as in história: far-MÁ-ci-a, PRÉ-di-o, ro-do-vi-Á-ri-a. The word tá is the everyday clipping of está: the first syllable is dropped, and the remaining syllable is stressed and ends in a, so it needs its accent. The accent on à is a different kind: it does not mark stress or vowel quality, and it is explained in the next note on contractions.

Consonant spellings. The cedilla in praça and estação is the way to write the s sound before a, o and u (c alone would be k there). In fica, c before a is k. In esquina, esquerda and parque, qu before e or i is the k sound with a silent u; in quadra, qu before a is pronounced kw, so the u is heard. Before e or i, g is the zh sound (longe), but g before r (igreja) or before o (chego) is the hard g, and j is always zh. The digraph ch is the sh sound: chego, SHE-goo. The loan word shopping keeps the English sh. Double rr between vowels is the strong r (correio), and ss between vowels is the s sound (atravessar).

Sounds that depend on position. Before the sound i, t becomes ch and d becomes j: direita is ji-REI-ta, frente is FREN-chi, and the weak final e is said i, so parque is PAR-ki and longe is LÕ-zhi. A final l is said w: hospital is oss-pi-TAW. The letters n and m after a vowel and before a consonant only nasalize the vowel: banco, ponto, longe, frente and entre contain a nasal vowel, with no n sound of its own. An h is silent. Use the table as a check: for every word in this lesson you should be able to rebuild the written form from the sound, and the sound from the written form.

grammar.title: Going, being and staying: ir, estar and ficar
grammar.explanation:
Two different questions can be asked about a place: where is something, and where is it going? English answers both with different verbs and different prepositions: 'I am at the bank' uses be and at, 'I am going to the bank' uses go and to. Portuguese makes the same split. Movement toward a place uses ir (to go) with a preposition of direction, a or para. A position uses estar (to be in a place right now) or ficar with em, which marks position. So the choice of verb and the choice of preposition travel together: ir goes with a or para, and estar goes with em.

Ir and estar are the irregular verbs from the grammar map: eu vou, você vai, nós vamos, vocês vão for ir; eu estou, você está, nós estamos, vocês estão for estar. Ficar is regular, a verb of the -ar family: stem fic- plus the endings fico, fica, ficamos, ficam. The c stays the k sound before o and a, as in fica; before e it would have to be written qu, which matters for the command form below. Literally ficar means to stay or to remain, and that is the logic of onde fica o banco?: a bank does not move, so it stays somewhere. English simply says 'is'. Use ficar for the location of things that stay put (buildings, streets, cities, rooms) and estar for the temporary position of people and movable things: o Pedro está atrás da porta, meu pai está no correio. With a person, ficar keeps its meaning of staying: eu fico em casa means I stay home (a decision or habit), while eu estou em casa means I am home right now.

There are three ways to say 'to' after ir. A is the formal one, and it contracts with the article: eu vou ao banco, eu vou à farmácia. Para is the most common in speech and shortens to pra or pro: eu vou pra escola. And in casual speech Brazilians also use em, as in eu vou no banco; teachers prefer ao, but you will hear no all the time. Para is also the natural choice before a city or country (vou para São Paulo). All three are understood everywhere. Arriving uses em or a too, never para: eu chego na praça, where the English is 'I get to the square'. Means of transport take de, 'of': de ônibus, de táxi, but on foot is a pé, literally 'at foot'.

grammar.title: Contractions and crase: do, no, ao, à, pelo, pro, daqui
grammar.explanation:
A preposition is a short word placed before a noun to say how it relates to the rest of the sentence: de (of, from), em (in, on, at), a (to), por (through, along, by), para (to, for). An article is the small word o, a, os or as, meaning 'the'. In Portuguese these small words are weak and fast, so when a preposition meets an article the two are fused into one word. This is a contraction. English only does it informally ('don't', 'gonna'), but in Portuguese it is obligatory: you always say no banco, never em o banco.

The pattern is simple. De and em lose their vowel and attach the article: de + o = do, de + a = da, em + o = no, em + a = na. Por becomes pel- before the article: por + o = pelo, por + a = pela. The preposition a is special because the article a has the same shape: a + o = ao, but a + a = à, one sound where there were two. The accent on à is called the crase, from a Greek word for blending. It does not mark stress or an open vowel; it records that two a's have merged, and it is said as one a, a little longer than the weak article. The same happens in plural: a + as = às, as in às dez, 'at ten'.

A test tells you when the crase is needed: replace the feminine noun with a masculine one. If the result is ao, the feminine version needs à. Vou ao banco, so vou à farmácia. Vire à direita works because direita is feminine and the article is understood: 'to the right'. No crase appears when there is no article to merge with: before a masculine noun (ao banco; and a pé, 'on foot', has no article at all), before a verb, since a verb never takes an article, before a place name that takes no article (eu vou a Curitiba, eu vou a São Paulo, but eu vou à Bahia, since Bahia takes an article), and after para (para a farmácia, with no accent, since para is a different preposition from a and there is only one a to merge).

Spoken Portuguese goes further: para loses its first syllable to become pra, and para + o becomes pro, one syllable. Pra and pro are normal in speech and in informal writing, and pra can stand for para or para a, with the context deciding. Finally, de also fuses with adverbs of place: de + aqui = daqui, 'from here', de + ali = dali, 'from there'. You will hear longe daqui in every set of directions. Note that ao lado do banco contains two contractions: a + o lado, and de + o banco.

grammar.title: Prepositions of place
grammar.explanation:
To say where something is in relation to something else, English uses single words (near, behind, between) and phrases (next to, in front of, far from, on top of). Portuguese does the same, but the phrases are built on one pattern: a place word followed by a linking preposition, de or a, then the thing. The place words perto (near), longe (far) and atrás (behind) are adverbs, words that tell where, and they can stand alone: é perto, fica atrás. When they need an object, they add the link: perto de, longe de, atrás de. English also needs a link in 'far from' and 'in front of', but not in 'near the bank'; Portuguese always needs it.

The linking word de or a then contracts with the article that follows, by the rules of the last note: perto do banco, longe da praça, atrás da igreja, em frente ao hospital, em frente à escola. Em frente a is built from em frente (in front) and a (to). Casually you also hear em frente do banco. Ao lado de contains a contraction itself: ao is a + o, and lado means side, so it is literally 'at the side of'. Em cima de is 'in top of'. Entre is different: it is a single preposition, needs no link, and does not contract: entre a padaria e a escola.

For here and there, Portuguese has three words. Aqui is here, near the speaker. Ali is there, near enough to point to. Lá is there, farther away or somewhere else. With de they give daqui, dali and de lá. Stress also explains their spelling: aqui and ali end in i, so they are stressed on the last syllable by default and need no accent, but lá is a stressed one-syllable word ending in a and takes an acute.

Brazilians give short distances in blocks and minutes, with a before the distance: fica a duas quadras daqui, literally 'it stays at two blocks from here'; fica a cinco minutos a pé. Duas is the feminine form of dois, because quadra is feminine. Use ficar for buildings and streets and estar for people and movable things. In speech, onde é...? is also common for the same question.

grammar.title: Giving directions: the command form
grammar.explanation:
When you tell someone to do something, you use a form of the verb called the imperative mood, which the grammar map introduced as 'the mood for commands'. English needs no special form: the bare infinitive does the job, 'turn', 'cross', whether you speak to one person or ten. Portuguese does have special forms, and they change with who is addressed. For giving directions to one person you use the command for você, and that is what this note teaches. It is polite, not rude: giving directions in the imperative is exactly what Brazilians do, and por favor makes it softer.

The rule is: take the eu form of the present tense, drop the final -o, and add the opposite vowel. Regular -ar verbs take -e and regular -er and -ir verbs take -a. So virar (eu viro) gives vire, atravessar (eu atravesso) gives atravesse, continuar (eu continuo) gives continue, and seguir (eu sigo) gives siga. Why opposite? A regular -ar verb in the present has -a for você: você vira means 'you turn'. If the command used the same form it would be identical to the statement, so Portuguese swaps the vowel: vira is a statement and vire is an order. The swap is the same as the present subjunctive, a mood you will meet at the intermediate level, which is where these forms come from; for now treat it as a pattern.

Building the command from the eu form explains the irregular verbs. Seguir has an irregular eu form, sigo, so the command is siga, not 'segua'. In the same way fazer (eu faço) gives faça, ver (eu vejo) gives veja, ter (eu tenho) gives tenha and sair (eu saio) gives saia. A few verbs stand outside the rule: ir gives vá, ser gives seja and estar gives esteja. The sound must also stay the same, so spelling adjusts: chego becomes chegue, because g before e would be the zh sound and gu keeps it hard; fico becomes fique, because c before e would be s and qu keeps it k. This is the same c, g and qu rule from the first lesson.

You do not say você: the verb ending already addresses the listener. A negative command puts não before the same form: não vire à esquerda. To speak to several people, add -m: virem, sigam, atravessem. In informal speech, Brazilians often give directions in the plain present as well: você segue em frente e vira à esquerda. Put the direction after the verb: vire à direita, siga em frente, atravesse a avenida. Até means 'until' or 'as far as', and is written with an acute because it is stressed on the last syllable of a word ending in e. Por duas quadras says how far, literally 'for two blocks'.

To ask for directions, get attention first. Com licença is literally 'with license', license in the old sense of permission: you are asking for permission to interrupt or to get past. Moço and moça, literally 'young man' and 'young woman', are polite ways to address a stranger. Then ask onde fica...? ('where stays...?') or como eu chego...? ('how do I arrive...?').

rows: -ar verb: opposite vowel e; ss stays
-ir verb: opposite vowel a; irregular eu form carries over
gu keeps the g hard before e
qu keeps the k sound before e

grammar.title: Ordinals: primeiro, segundo, terceiro
grammar.explanation:
A cardinal number says how many (um, dois, três). An ordinal number says which position in a sequence: first, second, third. English forms most ordinals by adding -th (fourth, fifth) and keeps three irregular ones (first, second, third). Portuguese ordinals are adjectives, so they follow the agreement rule you already know: they take the gender and number of the noun, with the endings o and a. The feminine forms are primeira, segunda, terceira, quarta and quinta.

The position is the same as in English: the ordinal comes before the noun. A direction word comes after the whole phrase: a segunda rua à esquerda is 'the second street on the left'. The noun's gender decides the ending: rua and quadra are feminine, so a primeira rua and a segunda quadra; semáforo and prédio are masculine, so o primeiro semáforo and o terceiro prédio.

With a preposition, the usual contraction applies: vire na primeira rua is em + a primeira rua, and o banco fica no terceiro prédio is em + o terceiro prédio. When the noun is obvious, it can be dropped, because the ordinal alone still carries the gender: vire na segunda means 'take the second', with rua understood. The ordinals beyond three, quarto, quinto and so on, work exactly the same way. You already met primeiro in the dates lesson, where primeiro de maio means the first of May.

culture.title: Streets, blocks and asking for help
culture.text:
Brazilian addresses start with the type of street, then the name and then the number, for example Rua das Flores, 120 or Avenida Paulista, 1000. People measure short distances in quadras, which means blocks, and in minutes on foot. In Brasília, a city planned from scratch, addresses use letter-and-number codes for residential blocks, and many visitors ask for directions to a quadra rather than a street.

It is normal to ask a stranger for directions. Start with com licença, which says literally 'with license', meaning with your permission, and use moço or moça, literally 'young man' and 'young woman', to get their attention. Brazilians are usually happy to help, but be careful with the answer fica logo ali, literally 'stays soon there' and meaning 'it is right over there'. It can mean anything from a few steps to several blocks, so ask for more detail if you are not sure.

Most people now use apps such as Waze or Google Maps to move around, but asking someone in person is still common. The word rodoviária refers to the main intercity bus terminal, which in many cities is the central point for traveling to other towns, because long-distance buses are the main form of public transport between cities in Brazil.

exercises.prompt: Match the Portuguese with the English
How do you ask 'Where is the pharmacy?'
exercises.explanation: Onde means where. Ficar literally means to stay or to remain, which is why it is the usual verb for the location of a fixed place: literally 'where stays the pharmacy?'

exercises.prompt: Why is metrô written with an accent, and why a circumflex?
choices: It is a contraction of two words
It is stressed on the last syllable, which breaks the default for a word ending in o, and its closed o takes the circumflex
exercises.explanation: A word ending in o is stressed on the second to last syllable by default. Metrô is stressed on the last, so it needs an accent, and the closed o takes the circumflex.

exercises.prompt: What does the accent on à in 'vire à direita' show?
choices: The vowel is stressed and open
Two a's have merged: the preposition a and the article a
exercises.explanation: This is the crase, from a Greek word for blending. It records that a + a became one sound, and it marks neither stress nor nasality.

exercises.prompt: In which word is the u after q pronounced?
exercises.explanation: Before e or i, the u of qu is silent (esquina, esquerda, parque). Before a it is pronounced: KWA-dra.

exercises.prompt: Why is the command for virar 'vire' and not 'vira'?
choices: Because command forms always end in -e
Because virar is an irregular verb
Because the command swaps the vowel: -ar verbs take -e, so it differs from the present 'você vira'
exercises.explanation: The command takes the opposite vowel: -ar verbs end in -e, -er and -ir verbs end in -a (siga). That keeps the command different from the statement você vira.

exercises.prompt: Which is the você command of chegar (eu chego)?
exercises.explanation: -ar verbs take -e, and the g needs a u before e to stay hard: chegue. Chege would be said with the zh sound.

exercises.prompt: Why do we say 'Eu vou ao banco' but 'Eu estou no banco'?
choices: Ir takes a preposition of direction (a or para) and estar takes em, which marks position
Ao is for masculine nouns and no is for feminine nouns
No is the formal form and ao is the casual form
Both mean the same thing and can be swapped freely
exercises.explanation: Going toward a place takes a (a + o = ao); being at a place takes em (em + o = no). Casual speech does let em replace a after ir, but not the other way around.

exercises.prompt: In 'ao lado do banco', what are ao and do?
exercises.explanation: Ao lado de is literally 'at the side of': a + o lado de. Then de + o banco gives do banco.

exercises.prompt: How do you say 'the second street'?
exercises.explanation: Rua is feminine, so the article is a and the ordinal takes the feminine ending: segunda.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence puts the crase in the right place?
exercises.explanation: Swap test: vou ao banco, so a masculine noun does not take à. Farmácia is feminine and takes the article a, so a + a = à. Curitiba takes no article, and a verb takes no article.

exercises.hint_en: I am at the bank now.
exercises.explanation: Estar marks position, so it takes em: em + o = no.

exercises.hint_en: She is going to the supermarket now.
exercises.explanation: Ir marks direction: a + o = ao. Casual speech also uses no (em + o), pro (para + o) or para o.
Por + o = pelo: going through or along.

exercises.prompt_pt: A farmácia fica em frente ___ banco.
exercises.hint_en: The pharmacy is across from the bank.
exercises.explanation: Em frente a + o = em frente ao. In casual speech you also hear em frente do.

exercises.hint_en: I go to the pharmacy. Use the contraction of a + a.
exercises.explanation: A + a merge into à, the crase. Swap test: with a masculine noun it would be ao.

exercises.hint_en: The bus station is far from here.
exercises.explanation: De + aqui = daqui: de loses its vowel and attaches to the adverb.
Eu viro, drop the o, add the opposite vowel e: vire.

exercises.hint_en: Go straight ahead until the traffic light.
exercises.explanation: Seguir has the irregular eu form sigo, and the command is built from it: siga. Continue works the same way.

exercises.hint_en: Turn onto the first street on the right.
exercises.explanation: Rua is feminine, so the ordinal takes the feminine ending: primeira.
